The first waited 30 seconds; the anchor arrived after that and was caught inside the second case's window. The event fired normally. The first window simply missed it. Four other cases with the same title all passed in this run, and in the previous run the anchor arrived inside 30 seconds

t: Is it broken, or not there yet?
d: In version documentation, half the feature description is wrong within six months. The date it appeared never is. And the date is usually what a verdict needs.
b: Engine manuals and release notes are the fastest rotting material there is. Six months in, half of it is wrong — APIs renamed, behaviour changed, things removed. One thing doesn't rot. When it appeared. This isn't trivia, it's grounds for a verdict The reason "added in 6.4" matters in QA is that when something won't reproduce, that single line is what decides whether it's a defect. One symptom can mean two things. Something that should work doesn't → a defect This version doesn't have it yet → not a defect You cannot tell them apart by looking. On screen they are both "it doesn't work." Logs don't help either — a feature that isn't there doesn't throw, it just does nothing. So when something won't reproduce, suspect the version first. Skip that order and you end up filing a bug report against a feature that does not exist, which is the kind of false positive that costs a developer's time. The reverse holds too. When something was removed doesn't rot either. Not knowing "removed in 5.8" means never finding out why something that worked fine has stopped. The newest document does not supersede the old one This is the counter intuitive part. We assume the latest document is a superset

d: The smallest chunk of text a model reads or writes; a single word often splits into several of them.
b: Pricing, context limits, and speed are all counted in this unit, and Korean text splits into more of them than English for the same content. tokens subword token count 서브워드 토큰 Token

d: The rule table and code that splits raw text into the units a model actually consumes.
b: Swap models without matching this and the output turns to garbage; the same sentence also costs a different number of tokens depending on which one is used. tokenization tokenize bpe 토크나이저 Tokenizer

d: The full list of tokens a model can recognize, usually tens to hundreds of thousands of entries.
b: Characters missing from it get shredded into more tokens, which is where a multilingual model's handling of Korean is actually decided. vocab vocab size 어휘 사전 어휘집 Vocabulary

d: One of the numbers inside a model whose value is set by training; their count is what people mean by model size.
b: The 27B in a model name means 27 billion of them, which roughly fixes how much memory and what class of GPU you need to run it. parameters params 매개변수 파라미터 Parameter

d: The trained parameter values themselves, saved as the files you download to run a model.
b: Releasing a model usually means uploading these files; the model is this pile of numbers, not the code that loads it. model weights weight file 가중치 파일 가중치 Weights

d: A list of numbers that places words or images so that similar meanings land close together.
b: Search, recommendation, and document retrieval all run on distances between these, and a paper saying representation learning usually means building better ones. embeddings embed vector representation 임베딩 Embedding

d: The maximum number of input plus output tokens a model can hold in view at once.
b: Most cases of an agent forgetting come from this limit, and since raising it costs money, memory and summarization schemes show up right beside it. context length context size long context 컨텍스트 길이 컨텍스트 창 Context window

d: Everything fed into the model for one turn: the question plus the rules, examples, and documents attached to it.
b: The same model performs very differently depending on it, and arguments over files like AGENTS.md are really arguments about what belongs in here. prompting 프롬프트 엔지니어링 프롬프트 Prompt

d: A very large neural network trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token, and therefore to write.
b: Most models in the news are variants of one design, so however different the names sound, they compare on the same axes: parameters, context, quantization. llm llms 언어모델 대규모 언어 모델 Large language model

d: A neural network built from stacked layers in which every token weighs every other token; the base design under almost all current LLMs.
b: The skeleton has barely changed since 2017, so what a new release actually changes is usually just the attention scheme and the routing. 트랜스포머 아키텍처 트랜스포머 Transformer

d: The operation that scores how much each token should read from every other token, then blends their information in those proportions.
b: Its cost grows with the square of the input length, which is why every long-context or inference-cost argument ends up back at this one step. self-attention self attention 셀프 어텐션 어텐션 Attention

d: Stored attention keys and values for tokens already processed, so generating each new token does not recompute the whole prompt.
b: This is why long chats slow down and GPU memory runs out: the cache grows linearly with context length and with every concurrent user. key-value cache kvcache KV 캐시 KV Cache

d: Generating one piece at a time by predicting what comes next, then feeding that prediction back in as input.
b: One wrong piece drags along everything after it, and both streaming output and tokens-per-second metrics fall out of this loop. autoregressive next-token prediction 다음 토큰 예측 자기회귀 생성 Autoregressive generation

d: Running an already-trained model to produce an answer, and the compute each of those runs burns.
b: Training happens once but this costs money on every request, which is why serving, edge, and quantization stories are all about shaving it. model inference inference cost 추론 비용 추론 Inference

d: The first and by far the most expensive stage, where a model learns general language ability from a huge unlabeled corpus.
b: Only a handful of labs can pay for this stage; nearly every other release is work layered on top of someone else's finished base. pre-training pretrain pretrained 사전학습 Pretraining

d: Taking an already-trained model and continuing training on your own data to specialize it.
b: When a company says it trained a model on its data, it almost always means this, not training from scratch, and both cost and ceiling differ. finetune finetuning fine tuning 파인튜닝 Fine-tuning

d: Training a small student model on a big teacher model's outputs to carry over as much behavior as possible.
b: When a small model punches above its size this is usually why, and the teacher's terms of service are the recurring dispute. knowledge distillation distill teacher-student 증류 Distillation

d: Converting model weights to fewer bits per value so the model needs less memory and bandwidth to run.
b: FP8, Q4 and GGUF tags on a model name all mean this; the model gets smaller and slightly worse, and how much worse is the whole argument. quantized quantisation model quantization 양자화 Quantization

d: An 8-bit floating point format that halves memory versus 16-bit while keeping enough range for most inference workloads.
b: An FP8 tag means the same model runs in half the memory, but native FP8 math needs a Hopper, Ada or newer GPU, so an A100 gets less out of it. fp8 quantization 8-bit float FP8 FP8

d: A single-file model format used by llama.cpp, packing quantized weights and metadata so a model runs without a Python stack.
b: A GGUF tag on a model page means it was uploaded to run on your own laptop, not in a datacenter; Ollama and LM Studio both load this format. gguf format llama.cpp format GGUF GGUF

d: A layout that holds many expert sub-networks and routes each token through only a few of them instead of all.
b: It backs claims of a huge model that runs fast, but all experts still sit in memory, so VRAM demand does not drop. 전문가 혼합 MoE Mixture of Experts

d: Fetching relevant documents first and pasting them into the prompt so the model answers from fresh or private data it never trained on.
b: Most quality problems live in retrieval, not generation, so when an answer is wrong, print what got retrieved before swapping the model. retrieval augmented generation retrieval-augmented RAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation

d: A fixed set of tasks every model is run against under the same rules, so scores can be compared across models.
b: Every -Bench in a paper title is one of these. Two numbers from two different suites are not the same measurement, however alike they look. benchmarking benchmark suite 벤치마크 Benchmark

d: An LLM program that takes a goal, picks and calls tools on its own, reads the results, and decides the next step over many turns.
b: When a title says agent, it is not about answer quality but about a loop that keeps going after failures, so the metric becomes task completion, not accuracy. llm agent ai agent agentic 에이전트 Agent

d: The code wrapped around a model that supplies its prompts, tools, procedure, retries, and stop conditions so a task actually finishes.
b: A score that jumps with the same weights usually means this layer changed, so decide first whether the claim is about the model or about the shell around it. agent harness scaffolding agent scaffold 하네스 Harness

d: Nvidia's programming layer for running computation on its chips; virtually every deep learning library sits on top of it.
b: The industry cannot leave Nvidia because of this layer, not the silicon; a post bragging about a hand-written kernel is bragging about work done here. cuda kernel nvcc CUDA CUDA

d: The amount of memory on the accelerator itself; weights and activations must all fit inside it before a model will run.
b: A claim that a model runs on 24GB is a claim about this number, and doing the arithmetic first saves a lot of wasted downloads. video memory gpu memory VRAM VRAM

d: A release where the trained parameter files are downloadable, so anyone can run the model on their own hardware.
b: It does not mean the code or the training data is open; the term gets used interchangeably with open source, but the license usually is not. open-weight weights released 가중치 공개 오픈 웨이트 Open weights

d: The property of one model handling inputs of different kinds, such as text, images, audio and video, within a single representation.
b: Image support is not one thing: check whether a model only reads images or also produces them before trusting the label. any-to-any omni model 멀티모달 모델 멀티모달 Multimodal

d: A model stating fabricated facts, citations, or APIs with the same confidence it uses for correct ones.
b: The danger is that it reads fine. Obvious errors get rejected; plausible ones ship into code and docs unchecked. hallucinate confabulation 할루시네이션 환각 Hallucination

d: A layout with a single stack and no separate encoder, where each position is masked to see only earlier tokens and predict the next one.
b: GPT, Qwen and DeepSeek all use it, so one-token-at-a-time generation is the root of how latency, streaming and per-token billing behave. decoder only 디코더 온리 구조 디코더 온리 Decoder-only

d: The part of a model that reads an input whole and turns it into meaning-bearing vectors, without generating anything itself.
b: A model built only from these, like BERT, cannot chat: it is meant for classification and search, and gets wired into a system differently. encoder-only 인코더 Encoder

d: An attention variant where several query heads share one set of keys and values, shrinking the cache instead of duplicating it per head.
b: It is close to standard now, so an older model without it burns several times the memory on a long conversation at the same parameter count. grouped query attention GQA Grouped-query attention

d: An attention implementation that tiles the computation in fast on-chip GPU memory, cutting slow memory round trips.
b: It made long contexts practical by cutting memory traffic without changing the math, and is now on by default in most engines. flash attention flash-attn FlashAttention FlashAttention

d: A way of encoding token order by rotating the vectors, now the default position scheme in most open models.
b: Most context-extension announcements are rescalings of this rotation, which is why quality slips beyond the length the model trained on. rotary embedding rope scaling RoPE Rotary position embedding

d: The share of a model's weights that actually take part in computing a single token, as opposed to the total it stores.
b: A name like 30B A3B means it stores 30B and runs 3B per token: read speed off the second number and memory off the first. activated parameters 활성 파라미터 수 활성 파라미터 Active parameters

d: The classic layout in which every weight participates in every token, with no routing or selective activation.
b: A 27B of this kind computes all 27B per token: slower but more uniform, and with far more finetuning and quantization precedent. dense transformer dense 모델 덴스 모델 Dense model

d: The total number of learned numbers a model holds; the B in a model name means billions of them.
b: It sets the memory bill: roughly parameter count times bytes per weight, so a 27B at 8 bits needs about 27GB before overhead. billion parameters 파라미터 개수 파라미터 수 Parameter count

d: Apple's machine learning framework for Apple silicon, plus the converted weight format models are published in so they run on it.
b: An MLX tag means the upload targets Macs; unified memory means the VRAM ceiling works differently there than on a discrete GPU. mlx-lm mlx format MLX MLX

d: Simulating low-precision rounding during training so the model still holds up after it is compressed.
b: A release that says quantization-aware is claiming its 4-bit build holds quality, unlike a checkpoint converted after the fact. quantization aware QAT Quantization-Aware Training

d: Freezes the original weights and trains a pair of small low-rank matrices beside them, which can be merged back in or swapped out.
b: The output is a file a fraction of the base model's size that you can ship, swap or stack, which is why most community tunes are shaped this way. low rank adaptation lora adapter LoRA Low-Rank Adaptation

d: A class of language models sized to run on a laptop, phone or edge device rather than a server rack.
b: They get chosen for latency, cost and privacy, not raw quality, so compare them against response-time budgets, not frontier models. slm on-device model 소형 언어 모델 Small language model

d: An architecture that carries a fixed-size running state instead of re-reading all past tokens, so cost grows linearly with length.
b: It is the line of work avoiding attention's quadratic cost on long inputs, and current releases usually hybridize the two. mamba ssm 상태공간모델 State space model

d: A generative approach that starts from noise and removes it over many steps to produce an image, video or audio clip.
b: Unlike models that append one token at a time, step count is both quality and cost, which is why releases lead with how few steps they need. latent diffusion 디퓨전 확산 모델 디퓨전 모델 Diffusion model

d: A model class that turns images into vectors and feeds them into a language model so it can answer about what it sees.
b: Screenshot-driven QA rides on these, and small text or coordinates break first at the vision side's resolution limit. vlm vision language model 비전 언어 모델 Vision-language model

d: Industry shorthand for the largest, most capable models currently at the performance edge, usually closed and served by API.
b: Policy and safety announcements use it to draw the line for what gets regulated; it marks a boundary more than a technical tier. frontier ai 프런티어 모델 Frontier model

d: A release further trained to follow instructions, as opposed to the base version that only continues text.
b: Chatting with the base build of the same model gives strange replies; nothing is broken, you just downloaded the wrong variant. instruct-tuned 인스트럭트 튜닝 인스트럭트 모델 Instruct model

d: The full set of weights saved at one point in training, which is the thing you actually download and run.
b: If the weights never ship, nobody can build on the paper; labs that also publish intermediate saves are worth far more to researchers. checkpoints training checkpoint model weights 체크포인트 Checkpoint

d: Everything done after the base model exists: instruction tuning, preference training, and safety work.
b: Two models built on the same base can behave nothing alike; the gap almost always comes from this stage, not from pretraining data. post training posttraining 후학습 포스트트레이닝 Post-training

d: The first post-training step, where the model imitates curated prompt-and-answer pairs written or vetted by humans.
b: This is where instruction-following manners come from: the difference between a base checkpoint and its Instruct sibling. instruction tuning sft 지도 파인튜닝 Supervised Fine-Tuning

d: A family of methods that freeze the original weights and train only a small added set, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude.
b: The acronym is a declaration that no full fine-tune happened, and the quality ceiling is not the same as one either. parameter-efficient tuning PEFT Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

d: Loads the base model in 4-bit and trains low-rank adapters on top, so a large model fits on a single consumer GPU.
b: Most claims of fine-tuning a 70B at home mean this; the trade is slower steps and some loss of precision. quantized lora 4-bit lora QLoRA QLoRA

d: Humans rank model outputs, a reward model learns those preferences, and the model is optimized to score higher against it.
b: Tone, refusals and safety behavior are shaped here; when a model suddenly gets more cautious after an update, this stage is the usual suspect.  RLHF Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback

d: A separate model trained on human preference data that scores candidate answers so RL can optimize against it.
b: If the scorer is biased, the trained model maximizes that bias: this is the usual road to sycophantic answers. reward modeling preference model 보상 모델 Reward Model

d: Samples several answers per prompt and trains on their relative scores, removing the separate value network that PPO needs.
b: It took PPO's place in reasoning-model training; seeing the acronym in a tech report tells you the model went through a reasoning RL stage.  GRPO Group Relative Policy Optimization

d: Trains directly on chosen-versus-rejected answer pairs, skipping the reward model and the RL loop entirely.
b: Simple and cheap enough that most community alignment tunes use it instead of full RLHF.  DPO Direct Preference Optimization

d: RL on tasks where a checker such as unit tests or a compiler decides right or wrong, so the reward needs no human and no reward model.
b: Sudden jumps in coding and math scores usually come from this setup; in QA terms, the test suite itself becomes the training signal. verifiable rewards verifiable reward RLVR Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards

d: A model exploits gaps in the scoring rule, driving the number up while abandoning the behavior that number was meant to stand for.
b: Code that special-cases the test to make it pass is this; when benchmarks rise while real use gets worse, suspect the scorer first. specification gaming reward gaming 보상 해킹 Reward Hacking

d: Training data generated by a model rather than collected from humans, then filtered before use.
b: Most post-training data is now made this way; the filter is the real product, and an unfiltered loop amplifies its own errors. synthetic dataset model-generated data 합성 데이터 Synthetic Data

d: Filtering duplicates, junk and harmful documents out of a raw corpus and deciding how much of each source to include.
b: It moves benchmark numbers more than architecture does, and it is the section tech reports most often leave blank. data mixture data filtering deduplication 데이터 큐레이션 Data Curation

d: Ordering training data from easy to hard, or shifting the data mix in stages, instead of feeding it all at random.
b: Late-stage runs often switch to a high-quality mix; the same data in a different order lands the model somewhere else. curriculum training data curriculum 커리큘럼 학습 Curriculum Learning

d: Empirical curves predicting how loss improves as parameters, data and compute grow, used to plan a run before spending on it.
b: It is the math behind budget-to-model claims; a release only becomes news when it lands off the curve. scaling laws chinchilla compute-optimal 스케일링 법칙 Scaling Law

d: A model that finished pretraining but got no instruction or preference training, so it continues text rather than answering.
b: When a repo ships both, the plain one is not a chatbot: it is raw material for someone else's fine-tune. base checkpoint non-instruct pretrained model 베이스 모델 Base Model

d: A model loses previously learned abilities while being trained on new data.
b: It is why a domain fine-tune often gets worse at everything else, and one reason people freeze the base and train adapters instead.  파국적 망각 Catastrophic Forgetting

d: When benchmark questions and answers already sit in the training data, so the score measures memorization rather than skill.
b: A high score on an old public benchmark is suspect for this first. Re-testing on fresh tasks often drops it sharply. contamination test set leakage 데이터 누출 데이터 오염 Data contamination

d: Feeding a released model a large domain corpus in the same unlabeled way, before any instruction tuning.
b: This is how medical, legal or single-language models appear; it needs orders of magnitude more data than a fine-tune. continual pretraining domain-adaptive pretraining 계속 사전학습 Continued Pretraining

d: Combining the weights of several models arithmetically to make a new one, with no additional training.
b: It explains how new models appear on hubs overnight: nearly free in GPU time, and impossible to trace which parent gave which ability. weight merging model soup weight averaging 모델 병합 Model Merging

d: A derivative of an open-weight model, redistributed after its refusal behavior has been stripped out or weakened.
b: An Uncensored tag means the weights differ from the original, so the base model's benchmark and safety numbers no longer describe what you downloaded. uncensored abliterated abliteration 언센서드 모델 Uncensored Model

d: A loop where a model generates attempts, a checker keeps the good ones, and those become training data for the next round.
b: Titles about self-evolving systems usually mean this loop; when the checker is weak, the loop just amplifies the model's own mistakes. self-improving self-evolving self-training 자기개선 루프 Self-Improvement Loop

d: Running a model behind an API or server so many concurrent requests are scheduled, handled, and billed.
b: Running a model once and serving thousands of users are different problems; titles with serving are about concurrency and unit cost, not model quality. model serving inference server 서빙 Serving

d: A quantization level storing each weight in about four bits, roughly a quarter the size of the original 16-bit model.
b: Q4 is usually the line between a 27B model fitting a 24GB GPU or not; suffixes like Q4_0 and Q4_K_M are different recipes at the same bit width. q4_0 q4_k_m int4 4-bit quantization Q4 Q4 / 4-bit quantization

d: The 16-bit floating point formats most released weights ship in, and the baseline that quantized versions get compared against.
b: This is the yardstick for model size: a 27B model in BF16 is about 54GB, FP8 halves it and Q4 quarters it. bfloat16 fp16 half precision BF16 BF16 / FP16

d: Managing KV cache in small fixed blocks like OS paging, so GPU memory is not wasted on reserved-but-unused space per request.
b: This is what made vLLM famous; claims about serving several times more concurrent requests on the same GPU usually trace back to it. paged attention PagedAttention PagedAttention

d: Grouping requests into one GPU pass and immediately slotting new requests into finished slots instead of waiting for the whole batch.
b: A GPU pass costs about the same for one user or thirty, which is why serving cost per user falls as traffic rises. in-flight batching iteration-level scheduling 연속 배칭 Continuous Batching

d: A small draft model guesses several next tokens and the big model verifies them in one pass, accepting the correct prefix.
b: A rare optimization that speeds up output without changing it, so it is the usual answer to why the same model suddenly got faster. draft model spec decoding 투기적 디코딩 Speculative Decoding

d: The opening phase of a request, where the whole prompt is computed at once to fill the KV cache before any token appears.
b: It is compute-bound, so a longer prompt directly delays the first character, and it is exactly the stretch that prompt caching bills away. prefill phase prompt processing 입력 처리 단계 프리필 단계 Prefill Phase

d: The delay between sending a request and the first token appearing, separate from how fast the rest streams out.
b: Perceived slowness lives here: a great tokens-per-second number still feels slow if the first token takes two seconds. first token latency TTFT Time to First Token

d: How many tokens per second a model produces, or how many requests per second a server sustains under load.
b: Per-user and whole-server numbers are both called throughput, so the first question about any benchmark is which one it measured. tokens per second tok/s tokens/sec 처리량 Throughput

d: How much data per second moves between memory and the compute units; for token-by-token generation this, not math speed, is the ceiling.
b: Generation is usually starved for data movement rather than math, and that single fact is why quantization and batching work at all. memory-bound bandwidth-bound 메모리 대역폭 Memory bandwidth

d: Keeping layers that do not fit in GPU memory on CPU RAM or disk and pulling them in when needed.
b: It makes an oversized model run at all, several times slower, which is why the same setup gets both it works and it is unusable reports. cpu offload layer offload offloaded layers 오프로딩 Offloading

d: An open-source serving engine built to pack many concurrent requests onto the same GPU efficiently.
b: It is the default in self-hosted serving, so papers and company posts usually use it as the throughput baseline they compare against. vllm serving vllm engine vLLM vLLM

d: A C++ inference engine that runs quantized models on ordinary laptops and desktops, on CPU or a single GPU.
b: Almost every run-it-yourself story sits on top of this: GGUF, Ollama and LM Studio are all layers above it. llamacpp llama cpp llama-cpp llama.cpp llama.cpp

d: A local runner that downloads a model and exposes it behind a local API with a single command.
b: Most I ran it locally posts mean this tool; the real work happens in the llama.cpp-derived engine underneath, so performance questions belong there. ollama run ollama pull Ollama Ollama

d: Reusing the computed state of a prompt prefix that repeats across requests, so repeated input is billed and processed cheaply.
b: For agents that resend the same system prompt and documents every turn, the cache hit rate is the bill: a miss can cost several times more. prompt cache context caching cached input 프롬프트 캐싱 Prompt Caching

d: API billing measured per million input and output tokens, usually priced separately with output several times more expensive.
b: Output costs several times more than input, so models that think longer bill more for the same question, and benchmarks now quote dollars next to scores. per token pricing price per million tokens 100만 토큰당 토큰 단가 Token Pricing

d: Running a model on the user's own laptop or phone instead of sending the request to a server.
b: No per-token bill and no data leaving the device, in exchange for that device's memory and bandwidth, which is why small MoE and 4-bit models keep shipping. edge inference local inference 엣지 추론 온디바이스 추론 On-Device Inference

d: The repeating cycle of think, call a tool, observe the result, and feed that observation back into the next prompt.
b: Cost is not one answer but how many times this cycle spins; runaway token bills almost always come from a loop that never decides to stop. react loop reason-act loop think-act-observe 에이전트 루프 Agent loop

d: Having the model call outside capabilities such as search, code execution, or file writes instead of answering from its own weights.
b: Failures split in two: the model choosing the wrong tool, and the tool returning junk, and debugging starts by deciding which one happened. tool calling tool call tool-calling 툴 유즈 Tool use

d: A convention where the model is given tool names and argument schemas up front and returns a chosen call with filled-in arguments.
b: The name and description are part of the prompt, so when a tool never gets called the culprit is usually that one description line, not the code. function call tool schema tool definition 함수 호출 Function calling

d: Forcing the model to emit JSON that matches a fixed schema instead of free prose.
b: It removes parse failures from a pipeline, but a schema that is too tight makes the model flatten what it actually wanted to say. json mode constrained decoding schema output 구조화 출력 Structured output

d: An open protocol that exposes tools and data sources in one shape so any client can connect to them the same way.
b: One server works across many clients, but every server you attach spends context on tool descriptions before the task even starts. mcp server mcp client MCP Model Context Protocol

d: Folders of instructions loaded only when relevant, injecting the how-to for a specific job at the moment it is needed.
b: A cheap way to add ability without growing the always-on prompt, though a vague trigger line means the file simply never loads. agent skill skill file skill.md 에이전트 스킬 Agent Skills

d: A convention file at a repo root that tells coding tools how to build, test, and follow that project's rules.
b: When an agent flails on an unfamiliar repo it usually cannot find how to build or test it, and rules only persist if they live in the repo, not in a chat. agents file claude.md repo instructions file AGENTS.md AGENTS.md

d: A tool that reads and edits a repo, runs its tests, and carries one instruction all the way to a committable change.
b: What separates it from autocomplete is not the output but the loop, and the dividing line is whether it can run the tests itself. code agent cli agent terminal agent 코딩 에이전트 Coding agent

d: An isolated environment where model-generated code or commands run, so a bad step cannot damage anything outside it.
b: The moment an agent gets a shell this becomes mandatory, and if the tool list includes deletes or pushes, an approval gate matters more than isolation. sandboxed execution code interpreter execution sandbox 샌드박스 Sandbox

d: Letting a model read the screen and drive mouse and keyboard so it can operate apps that expose no API.
b: It is the last resort for tools with no API: slow, brittle, and worth logging every step because a rerun rarely reproduces the same screen. gui agent browser agent screen control 컴퓨터 유즈 Computer use

d: Splitting long documents into retrievable units, where the size and overlap of the pieces decide what can be found at all.
b: A table or code block cut in half effectively disappears from search, and a surprising share of retrieval failures trace back to this step. chunk size text splitting document chunking 청킹 Chunking

d: A store that keeps text as numeric arrays of meaning and returns the entries closest to a query, fast.
b: It finds things that share no keywords, but it is weak exactly where you need a literal match, like an error code or an ID. vector store vector index 벡터 DB Vector database

d: A small model that takes the few dozen candidates from first-pass search and re-scores them against the query.
b: If only the top five reach the prompt, ordering is the answer, and bolting this on is usually cheaper than replacing the retriever. re-ranker cross-encoder reranking 리랭커 Reranker

d: Storing facts, preferences, and past decisions outside the session and pulling them back into the prompt when they are needed.
b: More stored memory is not better: one stale fact that never gets retired makes the model confidently wrong, and it will quote that fact as its reason. long-term memory memory store persistent memory 에이전트 메모리 Agent memory

d: Deciding what goes into each call and what stays out, treating the limited input window as a budget to spend.
b: It is not about writing a better prompt but about allocation: tool definitions, memory, and retrieved chunks all compete for the same room. context management context budget 컨텍스트 엔지니어링 Context engineering

d: The property of tasks that need tens or hundreds of chained steps, where one wrong turn early poisons everything after it.
b: Ninety-five percent per step is near-certain failure over fifty steps, so papers with this word are usually about recovery and stopping, not accuracy. long horizon multi-step task long-running agent 롱호라이즌 Long-horizon

d: Letting outside code own the order, branching, and retries across many model calls and tool runs.
b: The more decisions the model makes the more flexible it is; the more the code makes, the more it reproduces, and that line is the whole design. workflow orchestration agent orchestration pipeline orchestration 오케스트레이션 Orchestration

d: Splitting one job across several role-specialized instances that pass results between each other.
b: You gain parallelism but they also cite each other's mistakes as evidence; work that fails with one instance rarely succeeds just by adding two more. multi agent agent swarm agent team 멀티에이전트 Multi-agent

d: A child run spawned by the main session to keep its own context clean, returning only a summary of what it found.
b: The point is to offload long searching and take back a summary, with the catch that whatever the summary drops, the parent never sees. sub-agent worker agent delegated agent 서브에이전트 Subagent

d: A middle layer that picks which model each request goes to, based on difficulty, price, and latency.
b: It is where cost gets cut by sending easy calls to cheap models, and also a single point whose outage takes every downstream app with it. llm router model routing request routing 모델 라우터 Model router

d: A design that puts human approval in front of risky actions so the model cannot carry one out end to end on its own.
b: Most agent safety rests here, and a gate that appears so often people click it out of habit is a gate in name only. hitl 승인 게이트 사람 승인 휴먼 인 더 루프 Human in the Loop

d: An attack where text arriving as input overrides the instructions the developer gave the model and gets carried out in their place.
b: Instructions and data arrive through the same channel, which is why no clean fix exists; with any tool-using agent, start reading here. 프롬프트 주입 인젝션 공격 프롬프트 인젝션 Prompt Injection

d: A machine check such as tests, compilation, or rules that scores an agent's output and lets it pass only when the check holds.
b: Papers with a verification gate usually raise scores by adding a grader, not a better model, and the trick only works where success is machine-checkable. verification gate verifier-gated checker model 검증기 Verifier

d: An agent benchmark that hands the model a terminal and scores whether the task actually ended in the required system state.
b: It shows up constantly in agent posts. The score is produced by the harness, tools, and retry budget as much as by the model. terminal bench tbench Terminal-Bench Terminal-Bench

d: A coding benchmark built from real GitHub issues: the agent patches the repo and the project's own tests decide pass or fail.
b: Nearly every coding-agent launch quotes it. The 500-task Verified subset and the full 2,294-task set are different exams, so the variant decides the number. swebench swe bench swe-bench verified SWE-bench SWE-bench

d: The test set plus the scoring procedure a team runs to check whether a model or agent behaves as intended.
b: A benchmark is a public exam; an eval is the one a team writes for its own product. That is why numbers rarely transfer between companies. evals evaluation set 평가셋 평가(eval) Eval

d: A public table ranking models by their scores on one benchmark or a bundle of them.
b: The top entries usually differ by fractions of a point. Ask the gap size and the number of runs before reading rank as ranking. leaderboards 리더보드 Leaderboard

d: A scoring rule that samples k answers per task and counts the task solved if any one of them passes the tests.
b: Raising k can only raise the score, so pass@1 and pass@10 are not rivals. A code-generation number quoted without its k compares to nothing. pass at k pass@1 pass@k pass@k

d: A chess-style relative rating: two models answer the same prompt, the winner gains points and the loser loses them.
b: The gap converts to a win probability: 100 points means winning about 64% of the time, 20 points means 53% — a coin flip in practice. bradley-terry elo score 엘로 Elo rating

d: Using another model to grade outputs — scoring an answer or picking a winner between two — in place of a human rater.
b: Cheap and fast, but judges favor long answers, whichever answer came first, and their own family's style. Model-only grading bakes that in. llm as judge llm judge model-graded judge model LLM 심판 LLM-as-a-judge

d: A measure of how surprised a model is by the next token in a text; lower means it predicted that corpus better.
b: Quantization posts lean on it to claim almost no quality loss. It is tied to one tokenizer and one corpus, so it cannot rank two models. 혼란도 퍼플렉시티 Perplexity

d: Data deliberately kept out of training so the score reflects performance on examples the model has never seen.
b: Once you tune against it repeatedly it stops being held out. Scores that climb while real usage does not are the usual symptom. heldout set test split 홀드아웃 홀드아웃 세트 Held-out set

d: The share of tasks a model got right — the simplest possible score, and the easiest to quote out of context.
b: A headline 95.3% is half a fact. Task count, attempts per task, and whether partial credit counted decide if it compares to anything. raw accuracy 정답률 pass rate 정확도 Accuracy

d: A 2020 multiple-choice exam spanning 57 subjects, long used as the default proxy for a model's breadth of knowledge.
b: Top models all sit in the 90s, so it no longer separates them. A launch leaning on this number is telling you very little. massive multitask language understanding MMLU MMLU

d: A site where two anonymous models answer the same prompt and human voters pick the better one, aggregated into a ranking.
b: Human votes cover open-ended prompts no test suite can, but style and length preferences leak in, so it often disagrees with coding scores. chatbot arena lm arena LMArena LMArena

d: The fraction of head-to-head comparisons in which one model's answer was chosen over another's.
b: Beating B 60% of the time is not a score of 60. Swap the opponent and the number moves, so win rates only compare inside one table. winrate head-to-head pairwise comparison 승률 Win rate

d: The state where leading models all cluster near the ceiling, so the benchmark can no longer tell them apart.
b: This is why new -Bench papers keep appearing. On an old exam a one- or two-point gap is usually noise. saturated benchmark ceiling effect 벤치마크 포화 Benchmark saturation

d: Training or tuning aimed at a specific test until the score rises without the underlying capability rising with it.
b: This is how a top-of-the-chart model still disappoints on your own work. The only fix is re-measuring on your data. overfitting to the benchmark teaching to the test goodhart 벤치마크 과적합 Benchmark overfitting

d: An experiment that removes one component at a time and re-measures, to show which part actually produced the gain.
b: The first table worth reading in a paper. Without it you cannot tell whether the gain came from the new idea or from more data. ablations ablation experiment 어블레이션 Ablation study

d: Having people read the outputs and score or rank them — slow and expensive, but still the reference other scoring is checked against.
b: It is how you check whether automatic grading is right. If a write-up hides how many raters agreed, treat that number as soft too. human raters annotator human preference 사람 평가 Human evaluation

d: How well a model's stated confidence matches how often it is actually right — 80% sure should mean right 80% of the time.
b: Good calibration makes escalate-to-a-human-when-unsure a workable rule. Bad calibration makes that branch useless. confidence calibration calibrated 캘리브레이션 Calibration

d: The share of flagged items that were right, paired with the share of real ones that were caught; F1 folds both into one number.
b: Call every case negative for something that happens 1% of the time and accuracy reads 99%. That is how one accuracy number hides a useless detector. f1 score 정밀도 재현율 정밀도·재현율 Precision and recall

d: The reference number a new method is compared against — usually the prior approach, or the trivial one.
b: The size of an improvement is decided by what it was compared to. A weak baseline makes an ordinary result look large, so read that line first. baselines strong baseline 베이스라인 Baseline

d: Grading by running the output — code compiles, tests pass, the system reaches the required state — instead of reading it.
b: No grader taste enters the score, which is why code benchmarks lean on it. The flip side: anything the tests do not check counts as a pass. execution-based unit test evaluation 실행 기반 평가 Execution-based evaluation

d: A small, human-verified set of inputs with agreed correct answers, kept fixed so later versions can be compared against it.
b: Rerunning it after every prompt change turns a claim of improvement into evidence. Without one, progress and wishful thinking look alike. golden dataset gold set 정답셋 골든셋 Golden set

d: Whether re-running the same evaluation under the same settings lands on the same score.
b: Agent evals swing by points between runs. A score with no run count may simply be the best of several attempts. reproducible variance across runs seed variance 재현성 Reproducibility

d: Deliberately attacking a model before release, by people or automated attackers, and feeding the successful breaks back into fixes.
b: It is exploratory testing under another name; a release note that says red teaming happened but not what broke has told you only half of it. red team adversarial testing 적대적 테스트 레드팀 Red Teaming

d: A written scoring guide that fixes, item by item, what earns which score before any grading happens.
b: For LLM judging the rubric is the metric. An 8.7 with no published criteria has nothing to do with anyone else's 8.7. rubric-based grading rubric 채점 기준표 루브릭 Rubric

d: A claim that a method scores highest of anything published so far on a particular benchmark.
b: Without naming the benchmark and the setting it says nothing — often the claim holds on only one sub-split. state-of-the-art SOTA State of the art

d: The work of making a model behave according to the goals and norms intended by the people who built and deployed it.
b: A capability claim and an alignment claim are two different claims, measured differently, and the second set of numbers always lands later. ai alignment 얼라인먼트 정렬 문제 정렬 Alignment

d: Training where a model critiques and revises its own answers against a written list of principles, instead of humans labeling each one.
b: The rules are a published document, so a refusal can be argued against text rather than guessed at, and the loop scales without buying more labels. 원칙 기반 학습 헌법 ai 헌법적 AI Constitutional AI

d: An input that talks a model past its own refusal rules through role-play, encodings or long setups to get output it was meant to block.
b: Every new model grows jailbreak reports within days; the claim that something is blocked and the fact of it always run on a lag. jailbreaking 탈옥 프롬프트 dan prompt 탈옥 Jailbreak

d: Planting the instruction in a page, document or code comment the model will read later, instead of typing it to the model directly.
b: The user did nothing wrong yet the agent obeys a stranger's sentence, which is why the cause sits outside the session logs you are reading. 간접 주입 간접 인젝션 간접 프롬프트 인젝션 Indirect Prompt Injection

d: A checking layer outside the model that filters inputs and outputs with rules or classifiers, blocking or rewriting anything out of bounds.
b: It can be tightened in a day without retraining, so post-incident fixes usually land here, and so do the easiest bypasses. guardrail safety filter 안전 필터 가드레일 Guardrails

d: A separate small model that scores whether a text or image falls into a banned category, sitting in front of or behind the main model.
b: Its false-positive and false-negative rates, not accuracy, decide how the product feels; one threshold separates too strict from an incident. moderation api content classifier 콘텐츠 필터 안전 분류기 Safety Classifier

d: A model turning down harmless requests, a side effect that grows every time the safety settings are tightened.
b: This is why refusal rates ship alongside safety numbers: safer and less useful can be the exact same change viewed from one side. over refusal false refusal 거절률 과잉 거절 Over-refusal

d: Embedding a signal people cannot notice into generated output so a detector can later confirm where it came from.
b: Remover repos show up right next to it for a reason: a mark only counts if it survives editing and re-encoding, and most do not. watermark 워터마크 synthid 워터마킹 Watermarking

d: A provenance standard that attaches a signed record of how a file was captured, generated and edited, shared by cameras and editing tools.
b: Watermarking fights over erasure; this fights over whether the metadata is still attached, and a screenshot usually strips it clean. content credentials 콘텐츠 자격증명 C2PA C2PA

d: A contract option where API requests and responses are not stored after they are served, with no logs and no training copies kept.
b: This one line usually decides whether internal code or specs may go into a model at all, and it is often an opt-in tier rather than the default. zdr zero retention 데이터 미보존 제로 데이터 보존 Zero Data Retention

d: Data that singles out a person, such as names, contacts and account ids, which slips into prompts and logs far too easily.
b: Prompts are logs too: paste in a real bug report or repro steps and that log has quietly become a store of personal data. personally identifiable information 개인식별정보 개인정보 개인식별정보(PII) PII

d: Removing the influence of specific training data from a model that already learned it, without paying for a full retrain.
b: Weights are not a database with rows to delete, so a claim that something was removed almost always means approximately removed. unlearning 언러닝 학습 데이터 삭제 머신 언러닝 Machine Unlearning

d: Slipping crafted samples into training or fine-tuning data so the model behaves the attacker's way under one specific trigger.
b: In a world of downloaded datasets and other people's checkpoints, the giveaway is that the benchmarks look completely normal. poisoning attack 학습 데이터 오염 백도어 공격 데이터 포이즈닝 Data Poisoning

d: A document shipped with a model stating its intended use, data summary, limits and evaluation results in a fixed set of sections.
b: On a Hugging Face page this is where license and disallowed uses live, and the empty sections are exactly what the team did not check. 모델카드 모델 카드 Model Card

d: A public report covering a deployed system as a whole: safety evaluations, mitigations applied, and the risks that remain.
b: It is the thick PDF that lands on frontier release day, and its failure cases usually tell you more than the benchmark table does. 시스템카드 시스템 카드 System Card

d: A written commitment that ties risk tiers to specific security and deployment measures, triggered when a capability shows up in testing.
b: Each lab names its own version differently, and since it is a promise rather than law the lab grades itself, but the tier does change what ships. rsp preparedness framework frontier safety framework 책임 있는 확장 정책(RSP) Responsible Scaling Policy

d: The European Union regulation that sorts AI systems into risk tiers by use case and attaches bans or duties to each tier.
b: The same model is high-risk in hiring and unregulated in a game: the duties attach to where you put it, not to the model on its own. ai act 유럽 ai법 eu 인공지능법 EU AI법 EU AI Act

d: Pre-release tests measuring whether a model gained abilities that cause serious harm if misused: bio, cyber or autonomy.
b: These tables run the other way from benchmarks, since a low score is the pass, so reading a high number as an achievement gets it backwards. capability eval dangerous capability testing 위험 능력 평가 Dangerous Capability Evaluation

d: A model bending facts and judgments to agree with the user, a habit that hardens when preference training rewards agreement.
b: It is the costliest failure in review or QA work: an agreeable answer is agreement, not verification, so a pass is not a pass. sycophantic 시코펀시 아첨 편향 아첨 Sycophancy

d: Research that opens up which internal computations produced a given output, in terms a person can actually read.
b: Behavioral testing only reports how a model answered on the day; claims about why it answers that way mostly come from this line of work. mechanistic interpretability 모델 내부 분석 해석가능성 Interpretability

d: The term for low-effort generated output produced in bulk and dumped into search results, repos and feeds without review.
b: It is why anti-slop tooling keeps appearing: generation got cheap and the review cost is the only cost left standing. anti-slop 저품질 생성물 AI 슬롭 AI Slop

d: The dispute over whether copyrighted works may be used to train models, and whether rights holders can opt out or get paid.
b: It is usually why a model card's data section is blank, and a ruling can make already-released weights undistributable. 데이터 옵트아웃 텍스트 마이닝 예외 학습 데이터 저작권 Training Data Copyright

d: Confining an agent's shell, files and network access to an isolated environment so a mistake cannot reach anything outside it.
b: The autonomy scores agent benchmarks advertise come from inside a container; the same setup on a work laptop is a different claim entirely. agent sandbox sandboxing 격리 실행 에이전트 샌드박싱 Agent Sandboxing

d: A chip that runs one operation across thousands of cores at once; deep learning training and inference happen essentially nowhere else.
b: Most numbers on a model card translate into how many of these you must rent or own; parameter counts and quantization are that arithmetic. graphics processing unit h100 b200 GPU GPU

d: Google's in-house accelerator for deep learning, rented through its cloud rather than bought, and the main alternative to Nvidia hardware.
b: The name that always shows up as the alternative in Nvidia-monopoly stories; the real price of using it is porting your stack off CUDA. tensor processing unit TPU TPU

d: A raw count of floating-point multiply-adds, the shared unit for how much computation a training run or a single forward pass consumed.
b: A paper reporting 1e25 FLOPs is reporting a budget, and regulators draw their thresholds in the same unit, so the number turns up in law too. floating point operations petaflop exaflop FLOPs FLOPs

d: One accelerator running for one hour, the standard unit for pricing a training or fine-tuning run on the rental market.
b: An announced training cost is almost always this unit times an hourly rate, so knowing the going rate lets you check the claim in seconds. gpu hours compute budget GPU-시간 GPU-hour

d: Thousands to hundreds of thousands of accelerators wired by high-speed links so a single training job can span all of them.
b: Counting cards is the wrong metric: if the links between them are slow half the fleet idles, which is why vendors brag about interconnect speed. nvlink infiniband GPU 클러스터 GPU cluster

d: A memory standard that stacks DRAM layers right beside the compute die to reach bandwidth a normal module cannot.
b: Chip shortage stories are usually memory shortage stories; the queue forms at this part and the packaging that attaches it, not at the logic fab. high bandwidth memory hbm3e HBM High Bandwidth Memory (HBM)

d: An API mode that queues non-urgent requests and returns them within a day, typically at half the normal per-token price.
b: Evals, labelling, and bulk summarization do not need to be real time, so not using this mode means paying twice for the same work. batch inference batch endpoint 배치 API Batch API

d: The unit that prices model usage: input and output are billed by the piece, normally quoted per million, with output costing more.
b: Input and output are priced several times apart, so an app that stuffs documents in and one that writes long answers have different economics. price per token per-million tokens 토큰당 원가 Cost per token

d: Building one enormous processor from an entire silicon wafer instead of dicing it into many separate chips.
b: The pitch is to delete the interconnect problem outright, so when this word shows up in an Nvidia-alternative story, that is the claim being made. cerebras wafer scale engine 웨이퍼 스케일 Wafer-scale

d: The electricity a training or serving site needs, contracted in megawatts and increasingly the factor that decides where it is built.
b: The binding constraint has shifted from chips to electricity, which is why utilities and national governments now appear in AI infrastructure stories. megawatt gigawatt power constraint 데이터센터 전력 Datacenter power

d: The phase where a model is shown data over and over and its internal numbers are nudged until the predictions get better.
b: It happens once and then freezes into files, so the thousands-of-GPUs figures in the news are almost always this, not the cost of using the model. training run 모델 학습 학습 Training

d: A stack of layers that multiplies and adds numbers to turn an input into an output, with those numbers learned from data.
b: Everything in today's AI sits on this one structure, and a transformer is just one particular answer to how the layers get stacked. neural net 인공신경망 심층 신경망 신경망 Neural network

d: The umbrella term for models that produce new text, images, audio, or code instead of classifying or scoring what already exists.
b: When an announcement leans on this phrase it usually means a language or image model, and that quality gets judged by output rather than one accuracy score. genai generative model 생성형 인공지능 생성형 AI Generative AI

d: Steering a model by pasting a handful of worked examples into the input instead of changing the model itself.
b: Doing the same with no examples is called zero-shot, and this is the cheap move people tell you to try before reaching for fine-tuning. few shot zero-shot one-shot in-context learning 퓨샷 Few-shot

d: A dial on how boldly the model picks each next piece: near zero it always takes the safest option, higher it wanders.
b: Low for code and extraction, higher for writing, and when someone reports that the output keeps changing this is the first setting to check. 샘플링 온도 sampling temperature 온도 Temperature

d: A sampling cutoff that keeps the likeliest candidates until their probabilities add up to a set share, and drops everything below.
b: It travels next to temperature but cuts in a different way, which is why guides for running models locally tell you to tune it alongside top-k. nucleus sampling top-k min-p Top-p Top-p

d: A cap on how many tokens one response may generate; hit it and the answer simply stops mid-sentence.
b: Most reports of an answer getting cut off trace back to this setting rather than the model, and it is a different number from the context window. max_tokens 출력 길이 제한 최대 출력 토큰 Max tokens

d: A string registered in advance so that generation halts the moment the model produces it.
b: It keeps the model from writing the other speaker's next line, and a badly chosen one chops valid answers off in the middle. stop token 정지 토큰 정지 시퀀스 Stop sequence

d: The instruction block placed ahead of the user's message that fixes the model's role, tone, and hard limits.
b: Most of a product's behavior lives here, which is why leaks make headlines, and it rides along on every request so you pay for it again unless it is cached. system message developer message 시스템 메시지 시스템 프롬프트 System prompt

d: A conversation carried on by re-sending the whole previous exchange along with every new message.
b: The model remembers nothing between calls, so every extra turn costs more and the oldest part of the exchange is what gets dropped first. multiturn conversation history 대화 기록 멀티턴 Multi-turn

d: Sending each generated piece the moment it appears instead of waiting for the whole answer to finish.
b: It makes the wait feel shorter without making it shorter, and it is why checking or filtering the full answer before showing it gets awkward. token streaming 스트리밍 응답 스트리밍 Streaming

d: The wall-clock time between sending a request and getting the answer back: what one user actually feels as slowness.
b: Throughput can improve while this gets worse: bigger bundles help the server and hurt the person waiting, so the two numbers have to be read together. response time tail latency 응답 지연 지연 시간 Latency

d: How many requests or training examples get processed together in a single pass.
b: GPUs get more efficient the more you bundle, at the price of waiting, and the number in a training paper is not the number in a serving config. batching batch_size 미니배치 배치 크기 Batch size

d: The property that the same input with the same settings can still come back different on each run.
b: It is why a test that passed yesterday fails today; temperature zero narrows it but never removes it, since GPU addition order shifts with batching. nondeterministic non-deterministic 재현 불가 비결정성 Nondeterminism

d: The document that says how far you may go with weights you downloaded: commercial use, redistribution, derivatives.
b: Released does not mean unrestricted: user-count caps, non-commercial clauses, and naming requirements are all common. apache 2.0 라이선스 조항 상업적 이용 모델 라이선스 Model license

d: Strictly, a release that opens the training code and data as well as the weights, not just the downloadable files.
b: Cards use the phrase loosely and most of the time only the weights are actually open; the license is what settles which one you are looking at. open source model open-source ai 오픈소스 모델 Open-source model

d: The de facto public warehouse where model files and datasets are uploaded, versioned, and downloaded.
b: When you hear a model has been released, it usually means it showed up here, with the model card, license, and quantized builds on one page. huggingface hf hub model hub 허깅페이스 Hugging Face

d: The format that stitches roles and messages into the single string a model was actually trained to read.
b: When a model you run yourself suddenly talks nonsense, a mismatched one is a common cause; it differs per model and ships with the weights. chat_template chatml instruct template 채팅 템플릿 Chat template

d: A model trained to generate a long chain of intermediate work before answering, trading tokens and latency for accuracy on hard tasks.
b: A thinking budget on a card marks this class; the hidden reasoning tokens are billed and delay the first answer, so it pays off only on genuinely hard work. thinking model 추론 모델 extended thinking thinking mode 리즈닝 모델 Reasoning model

d: One stacked block of attention plus a feed-forward part, repeated dozens of times to form the model, with the repeat count being its depth.
b: A 48-layer spec is a depth claim, and since layers run strictly in sequence, a deeper model of the same size pays more latency per token. layers transformer block 레이어 수 레이어 Layer

d: Parallel slices within one attention block, each computing a different relation between tokens before their outputs are concatenated.
b: It explains specs that list query heads and KV heads separately: sharing one KV set across several query heads to shrink the cache is what GQA does. multi-head attention heads multi-head attention kv head 어텐션 헤드 Attention head

d: The two-layer transform that follows attention in every block; it holds most of a model's parameters.
b: MoE replicates this part and nothing else, which is why expert count can grow while active parameters stay flat, and a card's SwiGLU refers to it too. mlp feed-forward feedforward swiglu 피드포워드 층 Feed-forward network

d: The small gate that picks which experts each token is sent to, and that choice is what keeps only a slice of the weights active.
b: MoE failures usually live here, not in the experts: routing collapses onto a few of them unless training adds a separate load-balancing loss. moe router gating network top-k routing expert router 전문가 라우팅 Expert routing

d: A stack that mixes layer types, running mostly cheap linear or state-space layers with a few full-attention layers kept for recall.
b: Releases claiming flat memory on long inputs usually mean this, and the cost is that serving stacks often need new kernels before they can run it at all. hybrid model mamba-transformer hybrid attention 하이브리드 모델 하이브리드 구조 Hybrid architecture

d: Restricting each token to a fixed nearby span instead of the whole sequence, usually with a few full-attention layers left in the stack.
b: It is the cheap route to long context: information outside the window only travels layer by layer, so distant needle-in-a-haystack retrieval breaks first. swa local attention window attention 슬라이딩 윈도 어텐션 Sliding window attention

d: The mechanism that tells an otherwise order-blind model where each token sits in the sequence.
b: It is the only channel carrying order, so a context window stretched several-fold usually means this scheme was rescaled, and accuracy leaks past trained distances. positional embedding position embedding 위치 임베딩 alibi 위치 인코딩 Positional encoding

d: The front end that turns an image into tokens the language part can read, usually trained separately and then attached.
b: It sets how many tokens one image costs, so raising resolution multiplies the bill, and small-text failures are usually its limit rather than the language model's. image encoder vision tower siglip 비전 인코더 Vision encoder

d: The raw per-token scores a model emits at each step, one per candidate, just before they become the probabilities sampling draws from.
b: Structured output, grammar constraints and speculative decoding all work by touching these, so an API that hides them keeps that control server-side only. logprobs logit bias log probability 로짓 Logits

d: An attention variant that caches keys and values compressed into a small latent vector and expands them back at use time.
b: It shrinks the KV cache several-fold at the same model size, which is why long-context releases advertise it in place of GQA. latent attention MLA Multi-head latent attention

d: The dedicated links wiring accelerators and servers together, carrying the results every card must exchange at each training step.
b: Nvidia sells this harder than the chips: when it is the bottleneck, adding cards stops shortening training, so read cluster claims for topology, not card count. nvlink infiniband rdma 인터커넥트 Interconnect

d: Splitting each weight matrix across several accelerators so a single layer is computed by all of them at once.
b: It is the usual way to run a model too big for one card; the number sits in your vLLM launch flags, and a wrong value leaves cards idle or blows past memory. tensor parallel tensor-parallel-size intra-layer parallelism 텐서 병렬 Tensor parallelism

d: Packing dozens of accelerators into one rack wired as a single unit, so the rack rather than the card becomes what you buy and deploy.
b: Recent announcements count racks, not cards, and the power and cooling arrive as a rack-sized requirement most existing datacenters cannot simply absorb. nvl72 rack scale gb200 랙 스케일 Rack-scale

d: Pulling heat off the chips with liquid instead of air, which stops being optional once a single rack draws tens of kilowatts.
b: When a new chip generation is slow to land, the blocker is usually the building, not supply: retrofitting plumbing is a construction project, not an order. direct-to-chip immersion cooling water cooling 액체 냉각 Liquid cooling

d: The delay when a request hits an idle server and the weights must first be loaded into accelerator memory before anything runs.
b: It is why serverless GPU is cheap and also why it feels slow: a 100GB model can take tens of seconds to answer, so you weigh that against paying to keep it warm. cold start latency scale-to-zero cold boot 콜드 스타트 Cold start

d: Renting spare capacity at a steep discount on the condition that the provider can reclaim the machine at a few minutes' notice.
b: It cuts training bills by more than half, but only if the job survives being killed, which is where all that advice about frequent checkpointing comes from. preemptible spot gpu preemption 스팟 인스턴스 Spot instance

d: Committing to accelerator capacity for months or years up front, buying both a discount and a place in the queue, used or not.
b: Those multi-billion-dollar cloud deals in the headlines are commitments to spend, not revenue already earned, and what is scarce is the slot, not the price. committed use capacity reservation reserved instance 예약 용량 Reserved capacity

d: A newer breed of provider that rents GPUs and little else, usually cheaper and quicker to allocate than the hyperscalers.
b: When an unfamiliar cloud name shows up in a training announcement it is usually one of these; the trade is raw machines you must operate yourself. gpu cloud ai cloud coreweave 네오클라우드 Neocloud

d: The full bill for running compute (hardware, power, cooling, staff, depreciation), and the number that decides whether to buy or rent.
b: Owning looks cheap only when power and headcount are left off the sheet; at low utilization the cards you bought are the most expensive option you had. tco cost of ownership all-in cost 총소유비용 Total cost of ownership

d: The ceiling an API puts on how many requests and tokens one account may spend per minute; go over and calls come back as 429s.
b: A new model is often unusable at launch because of this number rather than its quality, so when an eval run dies mid-way, check here before blaming the model. rate limiting tokens per minute tpm 레이트 리밋 Rate limit

d: Which country's servers your requests and stored data physically sit in, fixed by contract and law rather than by preference.
b: Enterprise adoption usually stalls here rather than on quality: the same model is simply unavailable to a company if there is no region it is allowed to use. data localization data sovereignty in-region 데이터 소재지 Data residency

d: The share of rented accelerator time that actually did math; the rest is the fleet waiting on data, storage, or the network.
b: You pay by the hour but get work only in proportion to this; MFU is the honest version of the number, and 40% counts as bragging. mfu model flops utilization hardware flops utilization GPU 가동률 GPU utilization

d: Knobs for how the next token is drawn: temperature flattens the probability distribution, top-p and top-k trim the candidate list.
b: Release notes that specify 'temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95' mean it: the same weights score differently when these drift, so published numbers assume them. top-k nucleus sampling 샘플링 파라미터 Sampling Parameters

d: The one-token-at-a-time stretch after prefill, where every step re-reads the full weight set and the cache out of memory.
b: This stretch is bound by memory bandwidth, not compute, which is why raw FLOPS figures mislead and why HBM specs decide serving speed. decoding phase generation phase 디코드 단계 Decode Phase

d: A step-by-step record of one agent run: every prompt sent, every tool called, and what each call returned.
b: An agent rarely fails the same way twice, so you find the step that broke by rewinding the recorded run, not by trying to reproduce it. tracing agent trace execution trace 트레이스 Trace

d: Replacing the earlier part of a long session with a summary so the run can keep going once the context window fills up.
b: Whatever the summary drops never comes back, and that is usually why a long run suddenly forgets what it was doing halfway through. compaction auto-compact 컨텍스트 컴팩션 Context compaction

d: An agent run that executes unattended in its own environment, reporting back as a pull request or a notification when it finishes.
b: There is no point to step in mid-run, so unless you narrow tool permissions and approval gates up front, review only happens after the fact. async agent cloud agent remote agent 백그라운드 에이전트 Background agent

d: Splitting a goal into small units with clear order and success conditions so each one can be run and checked on its own.
b: A bad split makes every later step fail faithfully; an agent that spins in circles is more often broken here than at the tool layer. decomposition plan-and-execute subtask 작업 분해 Task decomposition

d: The step size of each weight update, usually warmed up at the start of a run and then decayed along a fixed schedule.
b: It is why fine-tuning guides hardcode a number like 2e-5 with no explanation: too high and the model breaks what it knew, too low and the run changes nothing. lr schedule lr warmup cosine decay 학습률 Learning Rate

d: The rule that turns gradients into actual weight updates; AdamW has been the default for years, and Muon is the current challenger.
b: A release note that says 'trained with Muon' is a cost claim - same data, same size, fewer GPU-hours - and swapping optimizers means retuning the learning rate. adamw muon sgd 옵티마이저 Optimizer

d: One number for how far the model's predictions sit from the training data; it slides down on a healthy run and spikes when it breaks.
b: It is the gauge behind lines like 'we rolled back to a checkpoint from three days ago' - a spike decides whether days of GPU time get thrown away. loss curve loss spike train loss 학습 손실 Training Loss
